extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys and other patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing patent applications and drafting patent claims, including required parts of an application, claim theory, claim format, wording, and prosecution considerations across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required parts of a patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application will typically include: a request; a description; claims; drawings; and an abstract. Where an invention relates to nucleotide and/or amino acid sequences, a sequence listing, typically in electronic form, may also be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National/regional laws may demand various other documents and statements (power of attorney, inventor identity, entitlement, oath/declaration of inventorship). Requirements vary by country so the patent drafter should check the rules of the territory/ies in which protection is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of the request (application form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The request explicitly states that an applicant seeks patent protection and is signed by the applicant or its representative. Request forms generally contain: the title of the invention; the name and address of the applicant and their representative; an indication of the inventor; and information relating to the priority claim (application number and filing date of earlier application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All priority information should be included in the patent application, whether on the request form or in an application data sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: sufficiency and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The description discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely so that a person skilled in the art will be able to carry out the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve readability the description usually contains: title; technical field; background art; summary of the invention outlining scope and how it solves background problems; brief explanation of the drawings; detailed examples (embodiments) referencing the drawings. Examples often play an important role in meeting support and enablement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope and legal operativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims define the scope of exclusive patent protection in terms of the technical features of the invention; they are the legally operative part of a patent application and patentability is determined on the basis of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be clear and concise, and fully supported by the description. Choice of terminology should track through the description consistently; unsupported claims can be thrown out for lack of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings as visual support
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings provide visual support in describing the invention and often facilitate better understanding of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings may include figures, tables, flow charts and diagrams. A representative drawing is usually positioned on the front page of a published patent document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: concise summary for search/readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract is a summary (a digest) of the invention limited to a certain number of words and typically includes key features recited in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract is primarily an aid for those conducting patent searches and readers of patent documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check jurisdictional application format differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the five main parts are common, detailed format and section headings differ across jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some patent offices supply sample application forms. A Common Application Format (CAF) exists accepted by EPO, JPO, KIPO, CNIPA and USPTO to reduce filing burden across multiple territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial patent drafter questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inventor instructs to file, the patent drafter must ask: What has been invented? What is the essential inventive concept? Does the inventor know what they want to protect? How should we claim the invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these points informs claiming strategy and ensures drafting aligns with client's protection goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish invention, embodiments and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is a construct in the inventor's mind; an embodiment is a physical form; claims must protect at least an embodiment but ideally protect the invention itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are a written approximation of the abstract concept. Best claims protect the 'invention' so that physical embodiments cannot be made, used or sold without infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement between description and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must support the patent claims; after drafting claims and description, the drafter must ensure every claim is adequately supported in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In strictly evaluated jurisdictions (e.g., EPO) the description must specifically include at least one embodiment that demonstrates claimed combinations (e.g., glass table with four legs) to meet support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for a mix of broad and narrow claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters should aim at a broad set of claims covering various aspects at different levels of detail, while including narrower claims as fallbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader claims increase protection but risk invalidity; narrower claims may survive litigation. Prior art unpredictability and unpublished applications may affect scope; claiming strategy is complex and may be adjusted during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-elements rule for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To assert patent infringement, all of the elements of a claim must be reproduced in the third party's accused embodiment; comparison is done element-by-element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an accused product lacks even one claimed element (or has elements in different relationships), there is no infringement under the all-elements rule. Use this to assess claim coverage and potential circumvention by competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements may be structural (what they are), functional (what they do), relational (relationships between elements), activity (steps in process claims), intentional (purpose), or parametric (measurable properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose element types appropriate to the subject matter; e.g., activity elements often use gerunds for process claims; parametric elements specify values like melting point or resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: General claim format conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is traditionally written as a single sentence in the present tense, beginning with a capital letter and ending with a period; semicolons separate clauses and phrases; claims are numbered consecutively and appear in a separate 'Claims' section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although formats vary, many patent offices expect heavy punctuation, specific indentation, and separation from the description. In some offices (CNIPA, JPO, KIPO) claims appear before the description; in the US the distinction is by phrases like 'I/we claim'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parts of a claim: preamble, transitional phrase, body
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim generally has a preamble (identifies category of the invention), a transitional phrase, and a body (elements and limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble should be chosen at the right level of breadth; it may be accorded differing weight in litigation depending on jurisdiction. The body must recite elements and their relationships, not just a list of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: choose level of breadth carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble is an introductory noun phrase identifying the category (e.g., apparatus, method) and may include modifiers that narrow scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader preambles increase scope but risk unity objections (multiple inventions) and divisional requirements. Keep preamble consistent with title where appropriate; avoid accidental narrowing (e.g., claiming 'telephone' when the invention is the mounting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrases: open-ended vs closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended phrases (comprising, including, containing, characterized by) are inclusive and do not exclude additional elements; closed phrases (consisting of) limit the claim to only the recited elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'comprising' leaves room for additional elements (e.g., a cap); 'consisting of' excludes unrecited elements and is rarely used because infringers can avoid infringement by adding an extra element. Jurisdictions interpret phrases differently (e.g., 'comprising' in Australia may be narrow). Check jurisdictional interpretations before choosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the claim must interrelate elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The body recites elements and explains how they exist in relationship to one another; claims cannot merely be a list of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent offices often reject mere lists. Use proper connectors and relationships (e.g., 'a top configured to be supported by at least one leg'). Open/closed phrasing can also be used within the body to define element groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and layout of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are frequently more extensively punctuated than grammatically required: comma separates preamble from transitional phrase; colon separates transition from body; elements typically separated by semicolons with '; and' before the last; many offices require line indentation for each element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow expected punctuation and indentation to ensure claims are interpreted as intended and to avoid formal objections or rejections by patent offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements must demonstrate correct antecedent basis: introduce with 'a' or 'an' on first use and refer back with 'the' thereafter. Each new claim set must re-establish antecedent basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide proper antecedent basis can create ambiguity as to whether references point to the same element or different ones. Use numbering (first, second) or phrases like 'another' when needed to distinguish multiple instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain language and avoid archaic legalese where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'the' and 'said' are interchangeable, 'said' is increasingly old-fashioned; trend in many jurisdictions is toward plain language even in law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain language aids interpretation by patent examiners, courts, and lay juries (e.g., in the US). However, be mindful of jurisdictional expectations and any legal consequences of word choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments vs closed transitional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: You will almost always better serve the client's interests by amending claims to avoid prior art in a manner that still makes it difficult for a competitor to avoid the claim — usually by adding clarifying amendments rather than using a closed transitional phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed transitional phrases make avoidance easier for competitors; consider amendment strategy during prosecution to balance overcoming prior art with maintaining robust protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripheral claiming doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Most countries follow a peripheral claiming doctrine in which the claims establish the outer limits of patent protection; draft claims to set the limits of the scope of protection sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a few jurisdictions use a 'central claiming' doctrine. Be aware of doctrine in jurisdictions of interest and draft accordingly to avoid unintended scope issues.
